stories.headline: Oil climbed back over $90 and stocks slipped as the Iran deadline passed with no deal
stories.dek: Brent crude jumped about 2.7 percent to $90.87 a barrel on Monday. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 percent. A U.S.-Iran pause was supposed to end that day.
stories.caveman: A thin sea lane between Iran and Oman used to carry a huge share of the world's oil. That lane is the Strait of Hormuz. War has almost shut it for months. Monday was the day a June pause between the United States and Iran was supposed to become a real peace deal. It did not. Oil jumped. Brent, a world oil price, closed near $90.87. U.S. oil closed near $84.50. Share prices fell. The S&P 500 dropped about 0.5 percent. The Dow lost about 273 points. The 30-year U.S. government bond yield hit 5.31 percent, the highest since 2007. That means markets think inflation may stay high and the U.S. will keep borrowing a lot. This week shops like Walmart, Home Depot, and Target report how much people bought. A European Central Bank paper also warned that a crash in U.S. AI stocks would hurt Europe too.
stories.why_it_matters: When oil jumps and long-term borrowing costs jump on the same day, almost everything gets more expensive: fuel, food shipping, mortgages, and company loans. Ordinary households feel it first. Stock investors who cheered last week's softer U.S. price data just learned that a closed strait can undo a 'Fed will wait' story in one session.
stories.camps: Energy traders and oil firms like higher crude. Stock investors and households hate it. The White House says high pump prices are the cost of squeezing Iran. Iran says the strait will not reopen until the U.S. blockade ends. Some economists say cheering weak shopping as 'good for rates' is a trap: if people stop buying, jobs go. Climate and left-leaning critics say a fossil-fuel war is a tax on the poor.
stories.image_alt: A trader in a blue jacket studies falling market charts on several screens in a dark trading room

terms.explain: A narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf. Before the war, about one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil went through it.
A standard type of oil used to set world prices. When people say oil is at $90, they often mean Brent.
A basket of 500 big U.S. companies. If this number falls, many people's pensions and funds feel it.
The interest the U.S. government pays to borrow. When this jumps, mortgages and company loans often follow.
The main bank of the United States. It sets the price of borrowing money.
Europe's main bank. It warned that a crash in U.S. AI stocks would leak into European jobs and credit.

stories.headline: China's factories and shops both slowed in July, missing the forecasts
stories.dek: Factory output grew 4.5 percent from a year earlier, and shop sales grew only 0.6 percent. Typhoons and weak household demand are the main reasons.
stories.caveman: China is the world's second-biggest economy. On Monday its statistics office said July was a weak start to the second half of the year. Factories grew 4.5 percent from a year ago, down from 5.3 percent in June. Watchers had guessed 4.8 percent. Shops grew only 0.6 percent. Watchers had guessed 1.5 percent. Three typhoons hit the east and south. Millions of people had to move. That stopped some factories and some shopping. Money spent on buildings fell 6.7 percent in the first seven months. New-home prices are still falling. Households keep a lot of their wealth in apartments, so when homes slump, people spend less. Exports of AI gear still help factories. China ran another month with more than $100 billion more exports than imports. The government says it will spend more, but it has not announced a giant new rescue package.
stories.why_it_matters: If Chinese families stop buying, the whole world sells less steel, cars, chips, and clothes. A huge trade surplus also makes Europe and the United States angrier about tariffs. Workers inside China feel a property slump as empty flats and unpaid overtime.
stories.camps: Beijing says the foundation is still solid and weather was the problem. Independent economists say officials have been too slow to spend and too scared of a big stimulus. Export factories want more state help. Trading partners say China is dumping spare goods abroad because its own shoppers are tired. Left-leaning critics inside and outside China say the state keeps pouring money into factories and AI while households get crumbs.
stories.image_alt: Workers and an orange truck clean rows of solar panels at a large desert solar farm in Xinjiang, China

terms.explain: How much stuff factories make. If this slows, fewer parts, cars, and machines leave the plant.
How much people spend in stores and online. A miss often means households are nervous or poorer.
Money spent on factories, roads, and buildings. A drop means China is building less.
When a country sells more to the world than it buys. China's monthly surplus is still over $100 billion.
Home prices and building keep falling. In China this matters because homes are how many families store wealth.
Extra government money or easier credit meant to wake up an economy. Beijing keeps promising it in a timely manner.

stories.headline: Canada's inflation hit 3 percent as gasoline jumped after Hormuz trouble
stories.dek: Yearly prices rose to the ceiling of the Bank of Canada's target. Gasoline cost 25.7 percent more than a year ago. Core prices stayed near 2 percent.
stories.caveman: Canada counts prices every month. On Monday it said July prices were 3 percent higher than a year ago. That is the top of the Bank of Canada's 1-to-3 percent comfort band. Watchers had guessed 2.9 percent. The big reason was gasoline. Fuel cost 25.7 percent more than last July, after 20.5 percent in June. The war around the Strait of Hormuz and trouble in the Red Sea pushed oil up. Travel tours and airfares also rose. Soccer's World Cup helped fill planes. Food in shops actually slowed a bit. If you take gasoline out, yearly inflation stayed at 2.2 percent for a third month. The Bank of Canada decides rates again on 2 September. Most economists still think it will hold at 2.25 percent, because jobs and trade with the United States are shaky.
stories.why_it_matters: A 3 percent headline number sounds scary at the pump. But if the rest of the basket is calm, the central bank may not hike. Households still pay more to drive and fly. That hits people who must commute more than people who work from home.
stories.camps: Hawks say energy pain can leak into other prices and the bank should stay ready to hike. Doves say core inflation is near target and a hike would punish workers for a war they did not start. Oil companies profit. Climate campaigners say this is what a fossil-fuel shock looks like. The government is watching the U.S. tariff calendar, which could raise other prices later.
stories.image_alt: A person in a blue jacket fills a Honda Civic at a gas pump

terms.explain: A monthly basket of what households pay for food, rent, fuel, and more. If CPI rises fast, life feels more expensive.
Canada's main bank. It tries to keep yearly inflation near 2 percent, inside a 1-to-3 percent band.
Prices after you strip out jumpy things like fuel. The bank watches this to see if pain is spreading.
The interest rate the Bank of Canada sets. It is 2.25 percent now. The next decision is 2 September.
The fuel most cars burn. In July it was the main reason Canada's headline inflation hit 3 percent.

stories.headline: Russia's state development bank fired its chief economist after he said the war of attrition is being lost
stories.dek: Andrei Klepach told a May forum that Russia is falling behind the West, China, and even Ukraine. VEB confirmed on Monday that he is gone. He confirmed it too.
stories.caveman: VEB is a big Russian state bank that funds the government's projects. Its chief economist, Andrei Klepach, had the job since 2014. In May he spoke to a club of economists in Moscow. He said Russia is losing both the technology race and the money race. He said Ukraine has not collapsed, costs keep rising, and a social crisis may come when nobody expects it. Russian media only widely printed those words last week. On Sunday and Monday, people who know the bank told Reuters he was fired. One said the order came from above. VEB told TASS he is no longer chief economist and a successor is already picked. Klepach confirmed his dismissal to Reuters. He did not take back the speech. Russia's central bank has already said growth this year could be about zero. Ukrainian strikes keep hitting refineries.
stories.why_it_matters: When a state bank economist says the war is eating the country, it is not a tweet from the opposition. It is a warning from inside the machine. Firing him tells other officials: do not say this out loud. That makes honest numbers harder to find, and ordinary Russians still pay in prices, soldiers, and frozen wages.
stories.camps: The Kremlin wants the story to be that Russia is resilient. Klepach said the lag will keep growing even if the economy does not collapse. Independent Russian media treated the firing as punishment for truth-telling. Ukraine says the comments prove Moscow cannot outlast Western support. Western hawks will use the quote to argue for more sanctions. Peace advocates say it is more evidence that civilians on both sides are paying for a long war.
stories.image_alt: VEB.RF chairman Igor Shuvalov in a suit and lanyard, chin in hand, at a formal event

terms.explain: Russia's state development bank. It funds big government projects and is not a normal high-street bank.
VEB's chief economist from 2014 until this week. He said Russia is losing a war of attrition.
A fight won by who can last longer, not by one big battle. Klepach said Russia will not win that kind of fight.
The boss of VEB. Sources said he dismissed Klepach after an order from above.
A Moscow forum of economists and officials. Klepach's May speech was posted on its website.

stories.headline: Uber will put Zipline drones on Uber Eats and aims for a million deliveries a day by 2029
stories.dek: First flights start later this year in cities where Zipline already flies, including Dallas and Houston. Uber is also investing. The amount was not disclosed.
stories.caveman: Uber wants food to arrive in five to ten minutes. On Monday it said it will partner with Zipline, a drone company in San Francisco. Zipline drones will drop Uber Eats orders. The companies want one million drone deliveries a day by the end of 2029. First runs start by year-end in places Zipline already works, then dozens of U.S. cities. Uber did not say how much money it is putting in. Zipline recently raised $800 million and is valued at $7.6 billion. Uber has already poured more than $10 billion into robotaxis and other robot vehicles. It also has a smaller drone deal with Israel's Flytrex. Uber's own flying-taxi project, Elevate, was sold off years ago. Now Uber's trick is: do not build the robot. Put many robot companies on the app.
stories.why_it_matters: If drones take the last mile, some gig drivers lose shifts. Neighbors get noise, privacy questions, and stuff falling from the sky. Fast delivery also means more packaging and more pressure on restaurants. The promise is cleaner, quicker drops. The risk is that workers and streets pay so an app can shave minutes.
stories.camps: Uber and Zipline sell this as teleportation and zero-emission flights. Labor groups and delivery workers fear another automation squeeze after years of thin gig pay. Cities worry about airspace, crashes, and who is liable. Some climate advocates like electric drones versus cars. Others say the real prize is ultra-fast commerce, not the planet.
stories.image_alt: A white Zipline drone hovers over a porch after dropping a green Uber Eats bag by the door

terms.explain: A San Francisco drone company. It already delivers medicine in several countries and food in some U.S. cities.
Uber's food-delivery app. The company wants drones to fulfill some orders in five to ten minutes.
A flying robot brings your order. No human driver for that last stretch.
Getting snacks or meals in minutes, not half an hour. Uber's boss says this market may be bigger than classic food delivery.
Uber's chief. He told the Wall Street Journal that truly fast delivery can be the next growth engine for Eats.
A person paid per job by an app, often with few benefits. Drones compete with their shifts.

stories.headline: Nvidia will put $1.5 billion into a SoftBank-OpenAI power plant and lock up an Ohio data center
stories.dek: SEC papers say Nvidia will be the only compute supplier at OpenAI's Ports-Pike site near Cincinnati and may extend up to $105 billion in credit. A $33 billion gas plant is planned on old uranium land.
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes the chips that run most AI. On Monday it said it will invest $1.5 billion in SB Energy. That company is tied to SoftBank and OpenAI. The prize is OpenAI's Ports-Pike data center near Cincinnati, Ohio. Nvidia would be the only firm allowed to supply the computers there. Papers filed with U.S. markets police also describe up to $105 billion in credit to help build it. The site could grow from 4.25 gigawatts to 8 gigawatts. SB Energy wants a 9.2-gigawatt natural-gas power plant on land owned by the U.S. energy department. The land once enriched uranium for bombs and Navy submarines. The plant may cost $33 billion. Gas-plant costs have jumped 66 percent in two years. When many AI plants hunt the same gas, prices for homes could triple in some places, BloombergNEF has warned.
stories.why_it_matters: This is not a cute startup round. It is a plan to burn a lot of gas so chatbots can think faster. Nearby towns get construction jobs and dirtier air. Ratepayers may pay more to heat homes. Nvidia gets a captive customer. The climate math is ugly unless the power later shifts off gas.
stories.camps: Nvidia, SoftBank, and OpenAI say America must build or China will. Ohio officials often want the jobs. Climate groups and some local residents say a uranium-site gas plant is the wrong bet. Consumer advocates fear household bills will subsidize AI. Chip rivals say Nvidia is using money and credit to lock the whole stack.
stories.image_alt: Nvidia chief Jensen Huang in a black leather jacket speaking on stage with server hardware behind him

terms.explain: The U.S. company whose chips power most big AI systems. It is putting money and credit into this Ohio project.
A data-center and power developer backed by SoftBank and OpenAI. Nvidia is investing $1.5 billion.
OpenAI's planned computer farm near Cincinnati. Nvidia would be the sole supplier of compute gear.
A huge unit of electric power. One gigawatt can supply a large city. This site could reach 8 gigawatts of compute.
A power station that burns methane. Cheap and fast to build versus nuclear, but it still dumps carbon.
The U.S. office that watches stock-market filings. Nvidia's credit promise showed up in those papers.

stories.headline: Groq raised $350 million to finish its pivot from homemade AI chips to renting Nvidia clouds
stories.dek: The round values the company at $3.5 billion, about half of last September. Nvidia may join. Groq says this is a new company after it licensed its talent to Nvidia.
stories.caveman: Groq used to build its own AI chips, called LPUs, to race Nvidia. Last year Nvidia hired Groq's founder Jonathan Ross and other stars as part of a $20 billion licensing deal. Groq then became a neocloud: it runs data centers full of Nvidia machines and rents them out. On Monday it said it raised $350 million. Disruptive led. Nvidia plans to put money in too. The new value is $3.5 billion. Last September Groq was said to be worth $6.9 billion. A spokesperson said this is not a down round. It is a price for the post-deal Groq. In June it already raised $650 million. Together that is $1 billion this year. Groq says it has 13 data centers, more than 6 million users, and wants to grow from 54 megawatts to more than 200 megawatts in 2027.
stories.why_it_matters: The chip rebel became a landlord for Nvidia gear. That shows how hard it is to beat the incumbent. It also shows how much cash it takes just to keep the lights on in AI. If neoclouds never make free cash, the bill lands on workers, the grid, and later investors.
stories.camps: Groq and Nvidia call this a partnership to scale inference. Skeptics say Nvidia bought the threat, then invested in the leftover rental shop. Public neoclouds like CoreWeave already make investors nervous about debt and dying chips. Workers at old Groq chip lines lost the original mission. Customers just want cheaper, faster answers from models.
stories.image_alt: A simple illustration of layered white clouds on a pale blue sky, used to suggest cloud computing

terms.explain: A U.S. AI firm that once made its own chips and now rents Nvidia computers as a neocloud.
A company that buys Nvidia chips, puts them in data centers, and rents the time to AI users.
Using a trained AI to answer a question in real time. Training builds the model. Inference runs it.
Groq's homemade chip, meant to be fast at inference. The company no longer bets the whole firm on it.
When a company raises money at a lower price than last time. Groq says $3.5 billion is a new baseline, not a down round.
A unit of electric power. Groq wants to grow from 54 megawatts of computing to more than 200 by 2027.

stories.headline: Investigators say an unprecedented number of iPhone users got Apple's spyware alerts this weekend
stories.dek: Access Now's helpline saw 30 to 40 percent more cases than usual after Friday's wave covering 110 countries. Apple now puts the warning on the lock screen, not only in email.
stories.caveman: Apple sometimes texts people that a government-grade spy tool may be hunting their iPhone. On Friday it sent a new wave in 110 countries. Over the weekend, many more people than usual said they got the warning. Access Now, a digital-rights group, told TechCrunch on Monday that its investigators saw about 30 to 40 percent more people asking for help than after a typical Apple blast. Some had been warned before. The security firm iVerify also saw a flood. Apple now shows the alert on the lock screen, in Settings, by email, and on the web. That extra noise may explain some of the jump. It may also mean more people are actually being targeted. Citizen Lab researcher John Scott-Railton said the volume could reflect both bigger attacks and the new, harder-to-miss alerts. The message is blunt: this is probably not a random hacker. Take it seriously.
stories.why_it_matters: These tools are sold to governments and used on journalists, lawyers, exiles, and activists. If the wave is real targeting, more civil society phones are in danger. If it is partly better warnings, that is still progress: people cannot protect a phone they never knew was hunted. Either way, mercenary spyware is no longer a niche story.
stories.camps: Apple presents the alerts as a public service. Spyware vendors and some states say the tools catch criminals. Rights groups say they are used to crush dissent. Privacy hawks want a ban on commercial spyware. Some targets fear the lock-screen warning itself paints a mark on them. TechCrunch's earlier weekend desk piece already told users not to ignore the ping.
stories.image_alt: A finger on an iPhone screen showing Apple's red warning that state-sponsored attackers may be targeting the device

terms.explain: A high-confidence Apple warning that you, personally, may have been targeted. It now appears on the iPhone lock screen.
Spy software sold to governments. It can read messages, microphones, and cameras without the owner knowing.
A nonprofit that helps people under digital attack. Its helpline saw a record jump after Friday's Apple alerts.
A University of Toronto group that studies government spyware. Its researchers said the alert volume is striking.
The first screen you see before unlocking a phone. Apple now puts spyware warnings there so they are hard to miss.

stories.headline: The U.S.-Iran 60-day clock ran out. Trump said no extension and threatened to bomb Oman
stories.dek: Monday was the deadline in June's Versailles memorandum. Iran threatened to hit the U.S. blockade. Trump said he might bomb a U.S. ally if it gets in the way over Hormuz.
stories.caveman: In June, President Donald Trump signed a paper in Versailles with Iran. It paused the fighting and gave 60 days to finish a real peace deal and nuclear talks. That clock stopped on Monday. There is still no deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump told reporters the United States is not seeking an extension. A senior Iranian official told Reuters Tehran may use force to break the U.S. naval blockade if talks fail. Trump also threatened to bomb Oman, a U.S. partner that shares the strait with Iran, if Oman blocks American plans. He has floated making Hormuz U.S. territory. Iran says point 5 of the June paper gave it a role managing the waterway. Washington rejects that reading. Pakistan, which helped broker June's deal, said it is still trying to keep the chapter open. Thousands have already died in Iran, Lebanon, and neighboring states since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February.
stories.why_it_matters: When a ceasefire calendar dies, the next choices are uglier: more bombing, a longer blockade, or a climbdown. Oil, food shipping, and U.S. midterm politics all sit on this strait. Threatening Oman, a mediator, also tells other Gulf states that even friends can be targets.
stories.camps: Trump says Iran must surrender and pay. Iran says the U.S. started the war and must lift the blockade and pay for damage. Oman wants to keep a shared waterway from becoming U.S. property. Gulf civilians and ship crews want tankers moving again. Anti-war voices in the U.S. say the Versailles pause was a stall, not a peace. Hawks say any extension rewards Iran.
stories.image_alt: Families on a Gulf beach with large cargo and supply ships anchored offshore

terms.explain: The June 17 paper that paused U.S.-Iran fighting for 60 days. The clock ended Monday without a final deal.
When a navy tries to stop ships from reaching a country's ports. The U.S. says it is blockading Iran.
A Gulf country that shares the Strait of Hormuz with Iran. It has been talking about future shipping rules. Trump threatened to bomb it.
Money paid after a war for destruction. Iran wants the U.S. to pay. Trump says Iran should pay.
The French palace where the June pause was signed. The 60-day peace clock started there.

stories.headline: Kushner and Netanyahu agreed a U.S. general should watch Hamas disarm, before any Israeli pullback
stories.dek: After rare talks with Hamas in Egypt, Jared Kushner sat for hours with Benjamin Netanyahu. Hamas already said yes to the U.S. roadmap. Israel still wants weapons gone before any withdrawal or rebuild.
stories.caveman: Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner is trying to restart a stalled Gaza plan. On Sunday he met Hamas's political leader Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt. On Monday he sat for hours with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem. Netanyahu's office called the meeting deep and constructive. An Israeli official said both sides agreed: no Israeli pullback and no reconstruction until Hamas is disarmed across Gaza, including light weapons. A U.S. general would watch the handover. They also set up two working groups, one on guns and one on water and sanitation. Kushner told Fox there could be progress in as little as 30 days if both sides cooperate. Hamas had asked the U.S. Board of Peace to compel Israel to accept the 15-point roadmap, which pairs disarmament with Israeli withdrawal and a new Palestinian civilian administration. Netanyahu, facing a tough October election, had already rejected a pullout until Hamas is genuinely disarmed. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million people are now squeezed west of a so-called Yellow Line.
stories.why_it_matters: If rebuild waits for total disarmament, tents stay, winter comes, and Israel keeps occupying more than half of Gaza. If Israel withdraws without a real weapons plan, Israeli voters and hostages' families will explode. People in Gaza are not a bargaining chip, but that is how the calendar is being written.
stories.camps: Netanyahu's coalition says security first, rebuild later. Hamas says it already accepted the U.S. plan and wants pressure on Israel. The Board of Peace wants a demilitarized Hamas and a new Gaza committee. Humanitarian groups say linking shelter to a political disarmament test will kill more civilians. Israeli opposition and some U.S. Democrats say Netanyahu is dragging talks for the October vote.
stories.image_alt: Jared Kushner in a dark open-collar shirt, looking aside under blue event lighting

terms.explain: Trump's son-in-law and Middle East envoy. He met Hamas on Sunday and Netanyahu on Monday.
The U.S.-backed group writing the next steps of Trump's Gaza plan, including a 15-point roadmap.
Taking away a group's weapons. Israel says this must finish before any pullback or rebuild.
A line Israeli forces have used to push most of Gaza's people into less than half of the enclave.
Hamas's political leader who met Kushner in Egypt and said the group is committed to the U.S. plan.

stories.headline: Russia and Ukraine traded more deadly strikes a night after Moscow called Ukraine's attack the year's largest
stories.dek: On Monday officials said nine people were killed in Ukrainian strikes on Russia and at least four in Russian strikes on Ukraine. Kyiv's Pochayna book market still smoldered from Saturday.
stories.caveman: The air war did not pause for Monday. Ukraine said Russian drones killed two people in Sumy and two in Donetsk, and set 54 market stalls on fire in Sloviansk. A strike also damaged a civilian ship in Odesa. Russia said nine people died in Ukrainian strikes, eight of them in Belgorod, plus a woman in Astrakhan. This followed Saturday night, when Russia said Ukraine fired about 822 drones, 600 of them toward Moscow, the largest Ukrainian attack of 2026. Russian attacks that same night killed at least seven people in Ukraine and burned a famous second-hand book market in Kyiv's Pochayna district. Russia said it was aiming at missile and drone factories. Firefighters were still in the ashes. Ukraine has also been hitting Wildberries warehouses, which Kyiv says help the Russian army's logistics. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia launched more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided bombs, and 62 missiles at 13 Ukrainian regions last week.
stories.why_it_matters: Each largest-ever night is also a night of burned markets, buses, and houses. Deep strikes on both sides make a ceasefire harder and winter energy more fragile. When a book market burns, a city loses more than stock. It loses a cheap public square.
stories.camps: Kyiv says it hits military logistics, not civilians, and that some Russian deaths come from falling debris. Moscow says the same in reverse. Human rights groups say both are hitting civilian areas too often. War-weary Europeans want talks. Hawks on both sides say only more pressure works. Booksellers in Kyiv just want to reopen.
stories.image_alt: A low building burns at night behind a metal fence after a strike

terms.explain: A second-hand market in Kyiv. A Russian strike on 16 August burned stalls and books.
A giant Russian online shop, sometimes called Russia's Amazon. Ukraine says its warehouses also move military supplies.
A bomb steered after it is dropped, often from a plane. Russia uses many of them on Ukrainian towns.
A Russian region on Ukraine's border. Local officials said eight people died there in 24 hours.
Ukraine's president. He said 13 regions were attacked last week.

stories.headline: Trump ordered U.S.-South Korea drills cut back. Seoul started them anyway
stories.dek: The president cited his very good relationship with Kim Jong Un and Seoul's no thanks on Iran. South Korea's military said Ulchi Freedom Shield would run as planned from 17 to 27 August.
stories.caveman: Every summer the United States and South Korea practice defending against North Korea. This year's exercise is called Ulchi Freedom Shield. It runs 11 days from 17 to 27 August with about 18,000 South Korean troops. On Sunday President Trump wrote that the drills are costly and hostile to a North Korea that has been unthreatening while he is president. He said it was too late to cancel, so Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth must substantially reduce them. He also complained that South Korean President Lee Jae Myung would not join U.S. efforts against Iran. South Korea's defense ministry said the drills would proceed as scheduled. The Joint Chiefs told Reuters they started on Monday. North Korea had already called the exercises a rehearsal for invasion and fired missiles this month. About 28,500 U.S. troops are based in South Korea. Trump has long wanted Seoul to pay more and drill less.
stories.why_it_matters: Allies read these posts as: your security is a bargaining chip next to a photo with Kim. If the drills shrink, North Korea learns that angering Washington works. If they do not shrink, Trump looks ignored. Either way, South Koreans live next to a nuclear army that has been fighting in Ukraine.
stories.camps: Trump and some America-First voices say the drills waste money and insult Kim. South Korea's government wants the usual shield and is reviewing the post. North Korea always demands a halt. Japan and other U.S. partners worry the three-way military web is being pulled apart. Progressives in Seoul sometimes also dislike live-fire spectacles, but not because Trump likes Kim.
stories.image_alt: A U.S. armored vehicle with an American flag crosses a pontoon bridge during a drill, with a South Korean flag in the background

terms.explain: The yearly summer military exercise of South Korea and the United States, running 17-27 August this year.
Trump's Pentagon chief. Trump told him to substantially reduce the Korea drills.
North Korea's ruler. Trump says their relationship is very good and the drills send a hostile signal.
South Korea's president. Trump said Lee declined to join U.S. action against Iran.
About 28,500 American troops stationed in South Korea. Trump often argues over who pays for them.

stories.headline: Amazon is buying rare books, slicing off their spines, and scanning them to train AI
stories.dek: 404 Media hid a tracker in a bulk order and followed it to a Las Vegas warehouse called VGT3. Amazon says it buys books through commercial channels. It would not say how many it destroys.
stories.caveman: Amazon began as a bookstore. On Monday TechCrunch and 404 Media said it is now buying piles of printed books, cutting off the bindings, scanning the pages, and throwing the paper away. A bookseller agreed to hide a tracker in a rare book that was part of a bulk order. The tracker went to Amazon's VGT3 operation in Las Vegas. Workers there say that is all they do: receive books, rip spines, scan fast. The team's logo is a dinosaur holding a book. Amazon told reporters it purchases books through commercial channels to improve the products and services customers use. It did not say which AI models get the scans, or whether it skips the last copy of a scarce title. Why rare books? The open web is already eaten. Text from before 2022 is unlikely to be written by a chatbot, so it helps models avoid model collapse. Anthropic already faced a fight over pirated books. This pipeline, at least, buys the paper first.
stories.why_it_matters: Once a physical book is destroyed, nobody else can hold that copy. Libraries, scholars, and used-book shops lose supply. Authors are rarely asked. A company that once promised to sell every book is turning unique objects into private training fuel.
stories.camps: Amazon says this is legal shopping to make products better. Booksellers who saw weird bulk orders feel used. Authors and librarians call it cultural strip-mining. AI labs say they need clean old text. Copyright hawks note buying a book is not the same as a license to train forever. Some workers at VGT3 worried the warehouse would close when the book pile ran dry.
stories.image_alt: Floor-to-ceiling wooden shelves packed with old books and a white step ladder in a private library

terms.explain: An Amazon warehouse operation in Las Vegas that cuts bindings and scans books for data.
The text and images an AI system is shown so it can learn to write and answer. Unique old books are prized.
When new AI models train too much on other AI text and get worse. Pre-2022 books are a way around that.
A small newsroom that hid a tracker in a rare book and followed it to Amazon.
A unique number on a book. Workers reportedly scan these first, which supports the idea of a systematic sweep.

stories.headline: H.M. Wolfe's Daggermouth debuts at No. 1 on the hardcover fiction list
stories.dek: Publishers Weekly's 17 August issue, using sales through 10 August, puts the dystopian enemies-to-lovers novel on top in its first week, with about 30,900 hardcover copies.
stories.caveman: Last week a new hardcover shoved its way to the front of the U.S. fiction pile. Daggermouth, by H.M. Wolfe, is a 544-page dystopian romance from Scarlett Press. A mercenary is sent to kill the president's son, botches the job, and is forced to marry him. The publisher compares it to Conform meets V for Vendetta. Deluxe copies have sprayed edges and extra art. PW's hardcover fiction list for the week ended 10 August, printed in the 17 August magazine, puts it at No. 1 in week one. Nielsen figures on the list show about 30,941 copies. Kathryn Stockett's The Calamity Club slipped to No. 2. Caro Claire Burke's Yesteryear, a long-running hit, is No. 3. This is a different lane from last week's overall No. 1, a TikTok romantasy paperback. Hardcover is the expensive, bookstore-front table. Wolfe is billed as a USA Today bestselling author. The book came out 28 July.
stories.why_it_matters: When a dark-romance hardcover opens at No. 1, it shows that BookTok taste now buys cloth boards, not only cheap paper. Traditional literary hardcovers have to share the penthouse. That shifts what publishers pay for, and what stores stack by the door.
stories.camps: Romance and romantasy readers celebrate another win. Some literary critics roll their eyes at sprayed edges and enemies-to-lovers beats. Bookstores like the traffic. Writers in quieter genres say the lists now reward existing online fandoms. Nobody is making shoppers buy it. They are.
stories.image_alt: Black cover of Daggermouth by H.M. Wolfe, with a grey heart bound in red cord and two roses
stories.image_credit: Cover: Scarlett Press / Simon and Schuster

terms.explain: PW's weekly ranking of new expensive fiction. Daggermouth opened at No. 1.
H.M. Wolfe's July 2026 dystopian romance. A mercenary is forced to marry her target.
The imprint that published Daggermouth. Deluxe copies have sprayed edges and extra art.
A romance pattern where two people start as opponents. This book uses a forced marriage after a failed assassination.
The book corner of TikTok. It can still mint hardcover hits, not only paperbacks.

stories.headline: E.J. Swift won the Arthur C. Clarke Award for When There Are Wolves Again
stories.dek: The British climate novel, already a BSFA winner, took science fiction's most closely watched U.K. book prize on Monday. U.S. readers know Swift for eco-fiction that treats restoration as politics.
stories.caveman: The Arthur C. Clarke Award is the United Kingdom's main prize for the year's best science-fiction novel. On Monday it went to E.J. Swift for When There Are Wolves Again, published by Arcadia. The book already won the British Science Fiction Association's best-novel prize. It is an eco-novel about bringing wolves and wild land back, and about who gets a say when the climate breaks. Kim Stanley Robinson called it vivid. The Guardian called it an eco-masterpiece. U.S. prize culture still orbits the Hugo, Nebula, and Booker, but Clarke is the one many American SF desks watch each August. A climate restoration story winning now is not an accident. Publishers are still buying eco-fiction even as headlines fill with fires and floods. Swift is British. The readers, and the argument, are transatlantic.
stories.why_it_matters: Prizes do not just hand a check. They tell stores which climate novels to keep on the table. A wolf-and-rewilding book winning Clarke says the serious SF lane is still about land, animals, and power, not only spaceships.
stories.camps: Eco-fiction fans feel seen. Some SF purists still sniff at issue novels. Conservationists like the wolves. Rural communities in rewilding fights often do not. U.S. publishers will now pitch similar titles harder for 2027.
stories.image_alt: Cream book cover of When There Are Wolves Again by E.J. Swift, with a wolf sliced by tree-like colored lines

terms.explain: The United Kingdom's leading yearly prize for a science-fiction novel. It was announced Monday.
Novels that treat climate, land, and nonhuman life as the main plot, not scenery.
Letting land go wild again, sometimes by returning animals like wolves. The novel turns that into a political fight.
Another U.K. science-fiction prize. Swift already won it for this book before Clarke.
A famous American climate-SF writer. His blurb is on Swift's cover.

stories.headline: Riley Sager's tenth novel, The Unknown, sits at No. 2 hardcover fiction and No. 5 in the country
stories.dek: PW calls the Vermont island mystery a closed-circle whodunit. Sager has joked that the book is his Eras Tour: it nods to nine earlier thrillers. First editions have red sprayed edges.
stories.caveman: Riley Sager is the pen name Todd Ritter took in 2017 after earlier books under his own name and as Alan Finn. His tenth novel, The Unknown, came out 4 August from Dutton. In Publishers Weekly's 17 August bestsellers column it is No. 2 on the hardcover fiction list and the No. 5 book in the country. The plot: in 1926 five women vanished from a Vermont island commune of spiritual mediums. A century later, an actress filming the story gets stuck on the same island and people start disappearing again. PW's review said the twists are effective even if they are not Sager's wildest. First-edition hardcovers are deluxe: designed endpapers, a foil-stamped case, a shimmery jacket, and red-hued page edges. Sager told People the tenth book was meant as his version of Taylor Swift's Eras Tour, touching every earlier book. Closed-circle thrillers, one island, a small cast, no easy exit, are having a moment next to romantasy.
stories.why_it_matters: Sager's machine shows how adult suspense still prints money without TikTok fairies. Deluxe first editions also train readers to treat thrillers like collectible objects. That is good for hardcovers. It is pricey for anyone who just wants the story.
stories.camps: Sager's fans treat each August like a holiday. Some reviewers want bigger swings. Booksellers like a reliable hardcover that is not 600 pages of romantasy. Collectors care about the sprayed-edge color change from black to red. Literary prize culture mostly ignores this lane, which is why the unit sales matter.
stories.image_alt: Hardcover of Riley Sager's The Unknown, with a black tree against a red sky and red-stained page edges

terms.explain: A U.S. thriller writer. The Unknown is his tenth novel under the Sager name.
A crime story where the suspects are trapped together, often on an island. Nobody new can walk in.
Color on the sides of a book's pages. First editions of The Unknown use red.
The Penguin Random House imprint that published The Unknown on 4 August 2026.
A first printing with extras, foil, endpapers, sprayed edges, sold as the default hardcover.

stories.headline: Thousands on Indonesia's Flores island waited for aid as Independence Day met a 7.7 quake
stories.dek: The Saturday quake has killed at least 68 people and hurt more than 200. About 19,000 people are in shelters. Aftershocks passed 1,500. Isolated villages were still cut off on Monday.
stories.caveman: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit Flores island in eastern Indonesia early Saturday. On Monday, as the country marked 81 years of independence, thousands still sat in tents. The national disaster agency said at least 68 people were dead, more than 200 hurt, and some 19,000 in temporary shelters. More than 4,500 homes were damaged, plus 122 health sites, 252 schools, and 84 places of worship. People slept outside because aftershocks kept coming, about 1,576 by Monday, 54 of them felt. The provincial governor declared a 14-day emergency. Jakarta sent soldiers, police, planes, and more than 100 tons of aid. Field hospitals went up in Ruteng after the local hospital roof failed. Palue Island, near the epicenter, was reached only late Sunday after landslides. A clothing trader in Reo told AP his house is rubble and he needs food, medicine, and water. Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire.
stories.why_it_matters: A country with a huge military still could not get water to every village in two days. That is geography and inequality: Flores is poorer than Java, and hills plus aftershocks block trucks. Independence Day speeches do not pour concrete.
stories.camps: The government says planes and field hospitals are moving. Villagers in cut-off hamlets say they have not seen aid and some have gone hungry in the hills. Doctors on the ground asked for volunteers and medicine on social media. Disaster experts note Indonesia has lived this script after 1992 on the same island and 2018 in Sulawesi. Climate is not the quake. Poverty is why some houses pancaked.
stories.image_alt: A man in a maroon cap stands before a white columned house whose upper floor has collapsed in an earthquake

terms.explain: An island in eastern Indonesia. The 7.7 quake hit here on 15 August.
Indonesia's national disaster office. It is counting deaths, tents, and aid tons.
A horseshoe of earthquakes and volcanoes around the Pacific. Indonesia sits on it.
A smaller earthquake after the big one. More than 1,500 have rattled Flores, so people will not sleep indoors.
A measure of earthquake size. 7.7 is major. This one was shallow, which makes shaking worse.

stories.headline: Rain helped Belgium's record wildfire, but Europe's fire summer kept killing and uprooting people
stories.dek: About 500 firefighters fought the High Fens blaze on Monday. Fires this year have burned 576,000 hectares in Europe, killed more than 20 people, and drawn an EU airlift to Belgium and Spain.
stories.caveman: Europe is in another climate-charged fire summer. On Monday, rain and cooler air helped crews in eastern Belgium's High Fens, the country's biggest modern wildfire, burning since Friday after 37C heat. It had eaten about 3,000 hectares and threatened the German town of Monschau. Some 500 firefighters from Belgium, Germany, and Luxembourg, plus EU planes from Sweden and helicopters from the Netherlands, Norway, and Germany, were on it. A ranger warned peat can smolder underground for months. In Greece, a Sunday fire on Salamina killed two people. A new blaze near Athens airport was knocked down in 30 minutes. In France, a Landes fire was finally controlled. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu offered 12 million euros for Gironde and Landes and was booed in Le Porge, where 183 homes burned last month. Spain's Aragon fire has burned close to 16,000 hectares and killed a soldier. The EU's fire service says Europe has already burned 576,000 hectares this year, twice Luxembourg, and last year was the worst on record.
stories.why_it_matters: Fires are no longer a southern holiday problem. Peat in Belgium, suburbs near Athens, and tourist coasts in Croatia are all on the map. Recovery money comes late. Renters and small towns get less help than rich coastal strips, which is why Lecornu got heckled.
stories.camps: Scientists tie the heat and dryness to climate change. Governments announce millions and EU planes. Residents say the state protected richer areas first. Farmers and soldiers are on the hoses because regular crews are not enough. Tourism boards want beaches reopened. Climate campaigners say this is the bill for delayed fossil-fuel cuts.
stories.image_alt: Charred ground and smoldering pines in thick smoke after a wildfire, with a burnt fence post in the foreground

terms.explain: A peat nature reserve in eastern Belgium. It is burning in the country's biggest modern wildfire.
When fire sinks into old wet soil that has dried. It can burn unseen for weeks and flare again.
The European Union's shared planes, helicopters, and crews. Belgium and Spain asked for them this week.
France's prime minister. He offered 12 million euros after wildfires and was heckled by people who lost homes.
The EU's fire-tracking system. It counts 576,000 hectares burned in Europe this year.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak is now the deadliest in the country's history, with 2,325 dead
stories.dek: Government data into Monday showed 4,945 cases. There is still no approved vaccine for this Bundibugyo strain. WHO says the pace is exceptional. The U.N. added $30.5 million on Friday.
stories.caveman: The Democratic Republic of Congo is fighting its 17th Ebola outbreak. Overnight into Monday the government said 2,325 people have died and 4,945 have been infected. That passes the 2,299 deaths of the 2018-2020 outbreak, until now Congo's worst. In the last counted day there were 101 new cases and 33 deaths. More than 1,000 people have recovered. 730 are in hospital or isolation. The virus is Bundibugyo, a rarer type with no approved shot or drug. Trials are running in Ituri, the epicenter. Some families have lost 15 relatives. WHO said last week set a record of 579 cases and 304 deaths. The outbreak was declared 15 May but likely started around a mining town in February. Roads are bad. Some health workers are on strike over unpaid wages. Rebels threaten teams. Rumors say Ebola is not real. U.N. relief chief Tom Fletcher put in another $30.5 million and 20 more staff on Friday and called for speed, scale, and solidarity.
stories.why_it_matters: A vaccine exists for other Ebola types. This type has none approved yet. That, plus war and unpaid nurses, is why a preventable hemorrhage disease is setting records. If it keeps this pace, WHO says it could rival West Africa's 2014-16 disaster, which killed more than 11,000.
stories.camps: Congo's government and WHO say they are scaling up. MSF says communities are still not being brought into the response. Unpaid clinicians cannot work for free forever. Mining towns want protection and still need to eat. Rich countries pledged money late. Conspiracy rumors fill the gap when trust is thin.
stories.image_alt: A health worker in a white protective suit sprays disinfectant into a freshly dug grave in red earth in Ituri, Congo

terms.explain: A severe virus that causes fever and bleeding. This outbreak is Congo's deadliest on record.
A rarer species of Ebola. There is no approved vaccine or treatment for it yet.
A province in eastern Congo. It is the epicenter of this outbreak.
A medical charity. Its emergency coordinator said community engagement is still too weak.
The share of confirmed patients who die. Here it has risen toward 46 percent, almost one in two.

stories.headline: The U.N. reached families trapped in a West Bank village, and said Gaza still cannot get the tents it needs
stories.dek: UNICEF delivered water and medicine in Qusra after a settler outpost boxed families in. In Gaza, partners have bought fewer than 30,000 tents against a need of 80,000 to 130,000, and most are stuck outside.
stories.caveman: On Monday the United Nations said its teams finally reached Palestinian families in Qusra, a village in the northern West Bank. Settlers had put up an outpost nearby, cut power and water, and kept people in their homes in a state of terror, the U.N. rights office said last week. UNICEF brought water, food, medicine, hygiene kits, and play kits for children. Three families were still surrounded on Monday. Municipal workers who tried to fix water and electricity were attacked by settlers. Some were detained by Israeli forces, spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. In Gaza, strikes continued west of the Yellow Line, where most of 2.1 million people now live in less than half the enclave. Winter is coming. The U.N. and partners have purchased fewer than 30,000 tents. They need 80,000 to 130,000. Most bought tents remain stuck outside Gaza. Stronger building materials are still barred. Less than 40 percent of a $4 billion appeal for Gaza and the West Bank has been paid this year.
stories.why_it_matters: A siege of 15 people in one village is a warning about the new normal in the West Bank. In Gaza the math is colder: without tents, rain will soak a population already pushed into a smaller and smaller strip. Diplomats argue about who disarms first. Night temperatures do not wait.
stories.camps: Israel says it is fighting Hamas and policing illegal outposts is complicated. Settlers and their political allies want more land. The U.N. says civilians must be protected now, not after a perfect deal. Hamas blames the occupation. Palestinian families in Qusra asked only for water, power, and to leave the house. Donors have pledged billions they have not sent.
stories.image_alt: Two U.N. workers in blue vests inspect a large unexploded bomb on a ruined street in Gaza

terms.explain: A Palestinian village in the northern West Bank. Families were confined after a nearby settler outpost went up.
A settlement put up without full Israeli government approval. In practice many become permanent and squeeze Palestinian villages.
The U.N. office that coordinates aid. It is tracking Qusra and Gaza shelter gaps.
A line used by Israeli forces. Most of Gaza's people are now west of it, on less than half the land.
The U.N.'s funding request for Gaza and the West Bank this year. Less than 40 percent has been paid.

A Russian region on Ukraine's border. Local officials said eight people died there in 24 hours.
Indonesia's national disaster office. It is counting deaths, tents, and aid tons.

Taking away a group's weapons. Israel says this must finish before any pullback or rebuild.

A severe virus that causes fever and bleeding. This outbreak is Congo's deadliest on record.
Europe's main bank. It warned that a crash in U.S. AI stocks would leak into European jobs and credit.
Novels that treat climate, land, and nonhuman life as the main plot, not scenery.
The EU's fire-tracking system. It counts 576,000 hectares burned in Europe this year.
A romance pattern where two people start as opponents. This book uses a forced marriage after a failed assassination.
The main bank of the United States. It sets the price of borrowing money.
Money spent on factories, roads, and buildings. A drop means China is building less.
An island in eastern Indonesia. The 7.7 quake hit here on 15 August.
The fuel most cars burn. In July it was the main reason Canada's headline inflation hit 3 percent.
A person paid per job by an app, often with few benefits. Drones compete with their shifts.

How much stuff factories make. If this slows, fewer parts, cars, and machines leave the plant.
Using a trained AI to answer a question in real time. Training builds the model. Inference runs it.
A unique number on a book. Workers reportedly scan these first, which supports the idea of a systematic sweep.
A province in eastern Congo. It is the epicenter of this outbreak.
Trump's son-in-law and Middle East envoy. He met Hamas on Sunday and Netanyahu on Monday.
Hamas's political leader who met Kushner in Egypt and said the group is committed to the U.S. plan.
North Korea's ruler. Trump says their relationship is very good and the drills send a hostile signal.

A measure of earthquake size. 7.7 is major. This one was shallow, which makes shaking worse.

Trump's Pentagon chief. Trump told him to substantially reduce the Korea drills.
A second-hand market in Kyiv. A Russian strike on 16 August burned stalls and books.
OpenAI's planned computer farm near Cincinnati. Nvidia would be the sole supplier of compute gear.
Home prices and building keep falling. In China this matters because homes are how many families store wealth.
Getting snacks or meals in minutes, not half an hour. Uber's boss says this market may be bigger than classic food delivery.
A Palestinian village in the northern West Bank. Families were confined after a nearby settler outpost went up.
Money paid after a war for destruction. Iran wants the U.S. to pay. Trump says Iran should pay.
The European Union's shared planes, helicopters, and crews. Belgium and Spain asked for them this week.
How much people spend in stores and online. A miss often means households are nervous or poorer.
Letting land go wild again, sometimes by returning animals like wolves. The novel turns that into a political fight.
A U.S. thriller writer. The Unknown is his tenth novel under the Sager name.
A horseshoe of earthquakes and volcanoes around the Pacific. Indonesia sits on it.

A data-center and power developer backed by SoftBank and OpenAI. Nvidia is investing $1.5 billion.

France's prime minister. He offered 12 million euros after wildfires and was heckled by people who lost homes.

Extra government money or easier credit meant to wake up an economy. Beijing keeps promising it in a timely manner.
A narrow sea passage at the mouth of the Persian Gulf. Before the war, about one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil went through it.
A high-confidence Apple warning that you, personally, may have been targeted. It now appears on the iPhone lock screen.
When a country sells more to the world than it buys. China's monthly surplus is still over $100 billion.
The text and images an AI system is shown so it can learn to write and answer. Unique old books are prized.

Uber's food-delivery app. The company wants drones to fulfill some orders in five to ten minutes.
The yearly summer military exercise of South Korea and the United States, running 17-27 August this year.
About 28,500 American troops stationed in South Korea. Trump often argues over who pays for them.
Russia's state development bank. It funds big government projects and is not a normal high-street bank.
The French palace where the June pause was signed. The 60-day peace clock started there.
An Amazon warehouse operation in Las Vegas that cuts bindings and scans books for data.
Ukraine's president. He said 13 regions were attacked last week.
A fight won by who can last longer, not by one big battle. Klepach said Russia will not win that kind of fight.
A giant Russian online shop, sometimes called Russia's Amazon. Ukraine says its warehouses also move military supplies.
